summary: Describes a DDDS database that uses the DNS to store rules, with domain names as keys and the rules encoded as NAPTR records. It replaces RFC 2915 and so is the official specification for the NAPTR resource record.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3403 defines how the DNS stores rules used by the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS). A client looks up a domain name, gets a NAPTR record, and uses that rule to decide what name or service to look up next.

subtitle: How DNS stores DDDS rules that turn an identifier into the next name to look up.

tldr.problem: The Dynamic Delegation Discovery System needs a distributed place to store rules that map an identifier to data through repeated lookups.
tldr.mechanism: DNS stores the rules as Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) records. Each record orders a rule and gives an application-defined service, flags, and either a regular-expression rewrite or a replacement domain name.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3403 is the official NAPTR record specification and obsoletes RFC 2915 and RFC 2168. It defines the database format, not a particular application; it is meant to be read with the other DDDS documents.

today: RFC 3403 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2915 and RFC 2168. It is the NAPTR database specification in the DDDS series.

sections.title: The DNS as a DDDS Rule Database
sections.content:
DDDS maps a unique string to data by applying rules repeatedly until it reaches a terminal result. This RFC defines one database for those rules: the Domain Name System (DNS). The key is a valid DNS domain name, and a normal DNS query for that name returns Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) records.

The RFC defines a database that different applications can share; it does not define a particular application. NAPTR was developed to store rules for rewriting identifiers, and the broader DDDS series supplies the algorithm and application specifications. The RFC says the series documents need to be read together.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines how DDDS rules are stored in DNS. A client queries a domain name to retrieve the rules for that key.

sections.title: Keys, Records and Rule Ownership
sections.content:
A DDDS key is a properly formed DNS domain name. A client asks DNS for NAPTR records at that name, and the response is a series of rules. An administrator inserts rules by adding records to the relevant DNS zone; only the authority that controls the zone can set the rule for a key there.

Record values use UTF-8. Substitution expressions that process non-ASCII text must treat it as code points, and they must not depend on a particular POSIX locale. DNS records expire according to their time to live (TTL). If an application falls back to previously retrieved rules, it must check that every record is still valid; if any has expired, it must restart the algorithm.

Applications can avoid rule collisions by using separate DNS zones, writing expressions that distinguish their identifiers, or defining different Flags or Services values.
sections.plainLanguage: The domain name identifies the rules, and the operator of its DNS zone controls those rules. A client must not reuse a rule after its DNS lifetime has expired.

sections.title: The Six NAPTR Record Fields
sections.content:
The NAPTR DNS type code is 35. Its fields are ORDER, PREFERENCE, FLAGS, SERVICES, REGEXP and REPLACEMENT. ORDER is a 16-bit integer; records are processed from the lowest order upward. PREFERENCE is also 16 bits and ranks records that have the same order, with lower values first.

The application defines the meaning of FLAGS and SERVICES. REGEXP holds a substitution expression applied to the original identifier. REPLACEMENT holds a fully qualified domain name for a simple replacement. The two replacement fields are mutually exclusive: a record containing both is in error and should be ignored or reported as an error.

A client must not apply a regular expression to the result of an earlier rewrite. Every expression applies to the original string. This rule avoids the error-prone behavior of cumulative rewriting.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAPTR record contains six fields that order a rule, identify its application and describe its result. A regular expression works on the original identifier, not on a name produced by an earlier rule.

sections.title: Processing and Forwarding Records
sections.content:
A client must process NAPTR records in ORDER sequence. Once a match is found, it must not consider records with a different ORDER, though it may consider records with the same ORDER and different PREFERENCE values. PREFERENCE is not the DNS load-balancing mechanism; the RFC points to SRV records or multiple A records for that purpose.

DNS servers may include related records in the Additional section. Applications may inspect that section but must work when it contains no useful records. A particular application must define the domain for its initial key, valid SERVICES and protocol values, the result of its terminal rule, and how it uses FLAGS.

If a lookup after a rewrite fails, clients are strongly encouraged to report the failure instead of returning to an earlier rule path.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients follow the record order and use the application’s rules to decide which result applies. They must still work when DNS omits optional extra records.

sections.title: Examples of URN and Telephone-Number Lookup
sections.content:
The RFC marks its URN example as hypothetical. A client extracts the namespace from a URN, forms the key cid.urn.arpa, and asks DNS for its NAPTR records. The first expression returns example.com; a later record uses an application-defined terminal flag and identifies a host to query.

The E.164 example begins with a telephone number. The application removes punctuation, reverses the digits, inserts dots, and appends e164.arpa to form the DNS key. Returned records can produce a URI and identify the service protocol. The exact flags and service values are defined by the application, not by this database specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show applications turning a URN or a telephone number into a DNS key. The returned rules can then identify another name or a service URI.

sections.title: Security and Registry Considerations
sections.content:
NAPTR records can be signed and validated using DNSSEC. The RFC warns that putting identifiers from other naming systems into this database exposes them to attacks similar to those against ordinary domain names.

Applications should check regular expressions for safety rather than passing them blindly to an interpreter that can execute arbitrary code. Each application decides the values for FLAGS and SERVICES and whether those values need an IANA registration process; this RFC itself requires no IANA resources.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC can authenticate NAPTR data. Applications must also examine rewrite expressions carefully because an unsafe expression could be treated as code.

viz.caption: THE SIX FIELDS IN A NAPTR RECORD

items.title: ORDER
items.text: Records are processed from lower values to higher values.

items.title: PREFERENCE
items.text: Ranks records that have the same ORDER.

items.title: FLAGS and SERVICES
items.text: Their meanings are set by each application.

items.title: REPLACEMENT
items.text: Names the next domain for a simple replacement.
